title: Live commerce is 30-40% of e-commerce in China and still single digits in the US
dek: Whatnot started with Pokémon cards and grew into a platform doing $8 billion in annual sales by letting users sell to each other on video. Live commerce is already 30-40% of all e-commerce in China and still single digits in the US — that gap is going to close.
why: The founder's own account of the full path from Pokémon cards to $8 billion in GMV, plus the two most valuable points: trust and safety takes 40% of headcount, and AI is used to make people more efficient, not to replace them.
who: Founders and investors building in e-commerce, live streaming and marketplaces; product leads who care about small-business enablement, building trust and safety systems, and where the line on AI actually falls.
skip: The opening Pokémon card and domain-name stories can be fast-forwarded; start at 10:21 with the market read.

points.h: Not knowing the market was actually an advantage
points.body: Grant says they started out knowing almost nothing about the market — they had never heard of live shopping in Asia, and their impression of QVC was ‘grannies shopping on QVC’. David George says flatly that this may have been an asset rather than a liability: if you understand the market deeply, you iterate on what already exists instead of building something entirely new. Grant calls it a ‘1,000% advantage’, because users don't care about the market at all — they care about whether the thing is fun and whether it has value.

points.h: Live shopping isn't e-commerce, it's a mall
points.body: Grant likens Whatnot to walking through a mall: you know you want something, but not specifically what, so you go in, wander around, play for a while, and maybe end up buying a pair of shoes. Traditional e-commerce assumes you already know what you want to buy, so it just moves offline selling online and makes it more efficient — it's not good at discovery or entertainment. Live does the opposite: it expands demand, because you find things you didn't know you'd be interested in. David adds that this is closer to the demand expansion that came with the birth of the department store or the shopping mall than to an extension of e-commerce.

points.h: Over 80% of users buy nothing that day
points.body: Whatnot users spend about 95 minutes a day on the platform, a number already on the scale of social and entertainment platforms. But Grant stresses that on any given day the vast majority of people buy nothing — over 80% of users don't transact that day, they just come to watch, chat and play. So it's fundamentally an entertainment format, with shopping as one part of it. David says he himself spends a lot of time on it, both for entertainment and to transact.

points.h: Top sellers make over $100M a year at 20-40% margins
points.body: The biggest merchants on Whatnot can do over $100 million a year in revenue, with EBITDA margins of 20%, 30% or even 40%-plus. The platform did over $8 billion in sales last year, and has already done over $8 billion this year to date — growing fast — but the platform only takes a small cut. Grant says they don't plan to raise rates: let merchants keep the lion's share and the platform grows along with them. David calls it one of the least-reported stories in American small-business enablement.

points.h: From collectibles to more than 100 categories
points.body: Today Whatnot sells across more than 100 categories. Grant names a few: fresh fish shipped straight off the dock in San Diego, barbecue joints, golf — golf is growing several hundred percent year over year. Women's clothing is already the largest category, closer in shape to TJ Maxx, selling off-season inventory at good prices. His test is: anything worth opening a physical store for is a fit for Whatnot, because you can do that store visit from your couch on your phone.

points.h: Going global came with no localization problem
points.body: Whatnot now covers about 10 countries: North America (the US and Canada), five European countries, Japan and Australia. Grant says the most counterintuitive part is that it works exactly the same way in all of them as it does in the US — the same small businesses get created, the same collectibles, fashion and electronics, with highly similar dynamics. That's what convinced him live is a very durable shopping medium.

points.h: Trust and safety is 40% of the staff
points.body: Grant says trust and safety is roughly 40% of Whatnot's employees, a huge investment, because nobody wants to put their credit card somewhere they don't trust, let alone buy fresh fish from somewhere they don't trust. Mechanically they have a rules engine that processes billions of data points per second and can identify and act on bad behavior at sub-second speed: harassment in a livestream gets detected by an LLM, fed into the rules engine, combined with seller history and other signals, and programmatically warned, suspended or banned; late shipping and excessive refund rates run through the same system. David's analogy: this is Whatnot's police and judicial system, equivalent to running two New York Cities.

points.h: AI is for efficiency, not for replacing people
points.body: Grant says the platform is self-reinforcing: if someone livestreams with an AI avatar, users won't come back, and that's not a good business. The core of Whatnot is walking into a store, getting to know the owner, and getting to know the regulars. So good sellers don't want to remove the human part, they want to amplify it. AI lands on helping sellers run the business more efficiently: listing products, automatically inferring from the livestream the metadata the discovery system needs, and telling sellers analytically where they're doing well and where they can improve. They don't offer avatar tools, because that's not why users come to Whatnot.
